background: In September 2025, Prosper announced that it had detected unauthorised access to their systems, which resulted in the exposure of customer and applicant information . The data breach impacted 17.6M unique email addresses, along with other customer information, including US Social Security numbers. Prosper advised that they did not find any evidence of unauthorised access to customer accounts and funds, and that their customer-facing operations were uninterrupted.
Further information about the incident is contained in Prosper's FAQs .
how: In September 2025, Prosper announced that it had detected unauthorised access to their systems, which resulted in the exposure of customer and applicant information .
Prosper advised that they did not find any evidence of unauthorised access to customer accounts and funds, and that their customer-facing operations were uninterrupted.
outcome: 17,605,276 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.

The reported exposed data includes Browser user agent details, Credit status information, Dates of birth, Email addresses, Employment statuses, Government issued IDs, Income levels, IP addresses, Names, Physical addresses.
editorial: Read the accompanying statement carefully: no evidence of unauthorised access to customer accounts. That can be entirely true at the same moment that 17.6 million people's Social Security numbers, incomes, employment status and credit standing have left the building. Account access and data theft are two different claims, and only one of them was being answered.

A lending platform holds the most complete financial identity most people ever assemble in one place, and it holds it for applicants as well as customers. People who were declined, or who filled in the form and thought better of it, have no account, no login, no dashboard and no particular reason to have been watching for a notice. They are in the file all the same.

This is one of the few entries in this archive where the usual advice is insufficient. A government identifier cannot be reissued because it leaked, so the only durable control is limiting what can be opened in your name. A credit freeze at each bureau is free, takes a few minutes, and lifts again when you actually need credit.
It is the specific countermeasure for the specific data that left here, and it works whether or not anyone ever touches your Prosper account.

fields.name: Government issued IDs
fields.why: Passport and licence numbers are used to prove identity to banks and telecoms, and they are effectively permanent.

fields.name: Physical addresses
fields.why: Where someone actually lives. Combined with a name this moves the risk off the internet.

fields.name: Dates of birth
fields.why: One of the three things call centres ask to verify identity, and it never changes.

fields.name: IP addresses
fields.why: Approximate location at the time of use, and a way to correlate accounts across services.

fields.name: Names
fields.why: Turns an anonymous address into an identified person, which is what makes targeted phishing possible.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: The address becomes a confirmed, active target, expect more phishing, better aimed.

fields.name: Browser user agent details
fields.why: Adds detail to a profile that can be assembled from several breaches at once.

fields.name: Credit status information
fields.why: Adds detail to a profile that can be assembled from several breaches at once.

fields.name: Income levels
fields.why: Adds detail to a profile that can be assembled from several breaches at once.

actions: Consider a credit freeze. A government identifier cannot be changed, so limiting what can be opened in your name is the only real control.
Be sceptical of post and callers who already know your address, knowing it is no longer evidence of anything.
Expect better-aimed phishing. A message that already knows your name and where you have an account is the whole point of a breach like this.
